title: Boolean multivariate quadratic equations

problem.name: Boolean multivariate quadratic equations
problem.statement_latex: Given $m$ quadratic polynomials $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, find $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$ such that $f_i(x)=0$ for every $i$, or report infeasibility. The square case $m=n$ is a basic algebraic-cryptanalysis benchmark and a foundation for multivariate signature assumptions. Complexity is measured in elementary quantum gates and classical bit-operation time on the explicit polynomial coefficient list.

quantum.headline_latex: $O(mn^2 2^{n/2})$ gates, Grover search with reversible quadratic-equation evaluation.
quantum.details_latex: Schwabe--Westerbaan construct the equation-checking oracle with $O(mn^2)$ gates and $O(m+n)$ qubits; their space-efficient variant uses $O(n+\log m)$ qubits with the same asymptotic gate bound. QuantumBooleanSolve gives $O(2^{(0.462+\varepsilon)n})$ expected gates for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$ when $m=n$ and the system is $0.17$-strong semiregular. Its deterministic variant gives $O(2^{(0.47+\varepsilon)n})$ gates for $m=n$ under $0.13$-strong semiregularity. These bounds include Macaulay-system linear algebra and coherent testing of partial assignments.

classical.headline_latex: $\operatorname{poly}(m,n)+O(2^{0.6943n})$ time, Dinur multiple parity counting; subexponential time for sparse systems, Boolean tensor contraction.
classical.details_latex: Polynomial-time Gaussian elimination removes linearly dependent equations from the coefficient list; Dinur's randomized search algorithm then uses parity counts of partial assignments. If $m=O(n)$ and each equation has polylogarithmically many monomials, the counting reduction gives $\operatorname{poly}(n)2^{O(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$. With linear total variable--monomial incidence, an $O(n)$-size Boolean circuit gives $\operatorname{poly}(n)2^{O(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$. These sparse bounds take precedence for their input regimes. Dense systems satisfying the quantum semiregularity promise give the displayed $0.6943$ versus $0.462$ comparison.

strength.description_latex: Polynomial speedup through a smaller exponential constant for the dense promised regime, using amplitude amplification and algebraic preprocessing. Sparse explicit systems have subexponential classical bounds.

evidence.description_latex: Partial evidence: the quantum algebraic exponent uses strong semiregularity, while the classical parity-counting bound is a general upper bound.

hardware.description_latex:
Reversible polynomial evaluation and Macaulay linear algebra need fault tolerance and substantial workspace. Direct Grover search uses $n$ assignment qubits and polynomial ancillas; the algebraic algorithm has additional matrix-storage and reversible-linear-algebra costs.

{\small [Before ``ETH is false'', the general classical upper bound applied to sparse quadratic systems was $O(2^{0.6943n})$, compared with the claimed $O(2^{(0.462+\varepsilon)n})$ quantum bound under strong semiregularity.]\par}
